title: High, Low and Octaves
description: Why every C on the keyboard sounds like C, even when they're far apart.

steps.title: High and low
steps.description:
Pitch is simply how high or low a note sounds. Move right on the keyboard and notes get higher. Move left and they get lower.

The keys repeat in a pattern of 12, seven white and five black. Go up 12 keys from any note and you land on the same letter again. That jump is an octave.

steps.title: A low C
steps.description: Play C3, the C one octave below middle C. Let it ring and notice how deep and warm it is.
steps.hint: Find middle C, then go left to the next C down. It's always the white key just left of a pair of black keys.

steps.title: Middle C
steps.description: Now play C4, middle C. Same letter, one octave up. It sounds brighter, but it's still clearly a C.
steps.hint: Middle C sits roughly in the centre of the keyboard, just left of a pair of black keys.

steps.title: A high C
steps.description: Play C5, the next C up. That's two octaves above where you started. Higher again, and still a C.
steps.hint: Count 12 keys up from middle C, or just find the next C to the right.

steps.title: Low and high together
steps.description: Play C3 and C5 at the same time. They're 24 semitones apart, but they melt into each other. It almost sounds like one rich note.
steps.hint: The low C from earlier and the high C, with middle C sitting in between.

steps.title: Why octaves match
steps.description:
Every note is something vibrating. Go up an octave and the vibration gets exactly twice as fast: middle C is about 262 vibrations a second, and the C above it is about 523.

That clean two-to-one fit is why the two notes blend so well that your ear hears them as the same note, just higher or lower.

steps.title: Octaves work on any note
steps.description: It's not just C. Play E3 and E4 together, an octave of E, and listen for that same blend.
steps.hint: E is the white key just right of a pair of black keys. Play the one above middle C and the one 12 keys below it.

steps.title: How far is an octave?
steps.description: How many semitones do you count to go up one octave?
